title: Color Matters: Investigating Stress Recovery in VR-Simulated Interior Environments Using fNIRS and Anxiety Measures

findings.antecedent: PASSAT-C cognitive stress task (60-second mental arithmetic challenge with auditory pacing at 2.7-second intervals)
findings.consequent: Oxygenated hemoglobin (HbO) activation in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC)
findings.statement: The PASSAT-C stress induction task successfully elicited increased cortical activation in DLPFC during stress phase compared to baseline

sample.population: right-handed university students with normal color vision, no neurological or psychiatric history

findings.quote: activation increased in the DLPFC (t (9) = 4.83, p < .001)

scope_conditions.setting: immersive VR environment (windowless room, 3m x 3m x 2.8m, neutral gray floor/ceiling, Oculus Quest 2 headset)
scope_conditions.population: N=38 university students (20 males, 18 females), age 21-33, right-handed
scope_conditions.measurement_type: real-time continuous fNIRS recording during stress task

stimulus_description.delivery_method: VR screen display within immersive environment
stimulus_description.components: random single-digit numbers (1-9) appearing sequentially; participants compute sum of most recent number and preceding number

findings.mechanism: Executive control and cognitive processing engage prefrontal cortex networks involved in emotion regulation and working memory

theory_links.theory_name: Prefrontal cortex involvement in stress response

findings.antecedent: Red wall color (monochromatic, H=336.13, S=50, L=50, HSL color space) during 60-second post-stress recovery period
findings.statement: Red wall color produced significantly elevated HbO activation in DLPFC (M=0.06, SD=0.06) compared to white wall color (M=-0.15, p<.05)
findings.test_statistic: post-hoc paired comparison with FDR correction

instruments_used.name: fNIRS (KY-A, Wuhan YIRUIDE Group)
instruments_used.construct_measured: oxygenated hemoglobin concentration in prefrontal cortex

findings.quote: the red condition (M = 0.06, SD = 0.06) showed significantly greater activation than white (M = −0.15, p < .05)

scope_conditions.setting: VR immersive environment with isolated wall color manipulation

stimulus_description.delivery_method: monochromatic wall surface in VR headset display
stimulus_description.components: four walls rendered in single hue with constant saturation/lightness

findings.mechanism: Warm hues activate cognitive control and attentional networks, sustaining stress-related neural activity

findings.antecedent: White wall color (neutral, L=100, S=0, H=0, HSL space) during recovery
findings.statement: White wall color elicited lowest cortical activation in DLPFC (M=-0.15) compared to warm colors (red, yellow, purple)
findings.test_statistic: multiple post-hoc comparisons with FDR correction
findings.quote: white condition consistently eliciting the lowest activation
findings.mechanism: Low-arousal colors engage parasympathetic regulation and reduce prefrontal engagement

findings.antecedent: Red, yellow, purple, and blue wall colors (systematic hue variation, constant saturation=50, lightness=50) during recovery
findings.consequent: HbO activation in PreM&SMC (premotor and supplementary motor cortex)
findings.statement: Red color showed highest activation in PreM&SMC (M=0.21, SD=0.07), significantly greater than orange, yellow, purple, white conditions (all p<.05 or p<.001)
findings.quote: the red condition (M = 0.21, SD = 0.07) showed the highest activation, significantly greater than the orange, yellow, purple, and white conditions (p < .05, .05, .01, and < .001, respectively)

stimulus_description.components: seven monochromatic wall colors: blue, red, orange, yellow, green, purple, white

findings.mechanism: Warm hues enhance motor readiness and arousal-related motor system engagement

findings.antecedent: Red wall color during early recovery phase (T1: 0-20 seconds post-stress)
findings.consequent: HbO activation in frontal eye fields (FEF)
findings.statement: Red color elicited significantly greater FEF activation (M=0.40) compared to blue (M=-0.50), green (M=-0.54), and white (M=-0.59) during early recovery (T1)
findings.quote: during the early recovery phase (T1), the red condition (M = 0.40) showed significantly greater activation than blue (M = −0.50, p < .05), green (M = −0.54, p < .01), and white (M = −0.59, p < .01)

scope_conditions.measurement_type: fNIRS measurement during specific time window

stimulus_description.components: red hue with high visual salience

findings.mechanism: Red activates visual salience detection systems, causing early and heightened frontal eye field engagement in threat/attention prioritization
moderators_reported: recovery time window (T1 vs T2 vs T3)

findings.antecedent: Yellow wall color during mid-recovery phase (T2: 20-40 seconds post-stress)
findings.statement: Yellow significantly elevated DLPFC activation during mid-recovery (T2) compared to white (M=0.31 vs M=-0.17, p<.05)
findings.quote: in the DLPFC, during the mid-recovery phase (T2), the yellow condition (M = 0.31) showed significantly greater activation than white (M = −0.17, p < .05)
findings.mechanism: Yellow supports cognitive stability and executive function during sustained recovery

findings.antecedent: White wall color during late recovery phase (T3: 40-60 seconds post-stress)
findings.statement: White showed significantly higher FEF activation during late recovery (T3: M=0.42) compared to purple (M=-0.23, p<.05)

instruments_used.name: fNIRS
instruments_used.construct_measured: HbO in frontal eye fields during late recovery

findings.quote: During the late recovery phase (T3), white (M = 0.42) showed significantly higher activation than purple (M = −0.23, p < .05)
findings.mechanism: Late-phase white activation in FEF may reflect stabilization of visual attention systems as recovery progresses

findings.antecedent: All wall colors (blue, red, orange, yellow, green, purple, white) - main time effect across recovery phases
findings.consequent: HbO activation in PreM&SMC over temporal recovery phases (T1, T2, T3)
findings.statement: Significant main effect of time on PreM&SMC activation: T2 (mid-recovery, M=0.29) showed peak activation, significantly greater than T1 (M=-0.12, p<.05) and T3 (M=-0.19, p<.05)
findings.quote: A significant main effect of Time was observed in the PreM&SMC (F(2, 72) = 4.70, p < .05, η² = 0.13). Post hoc analyses with FDR correction revealed that activation during the second interval (T2, M = 0.29) was significantly greater than both the first (T1, M = −0.12, p < .05) and the final (T3, M = −0.19, p < .05) intervals

scope_conditions.duration: entire 60-second recovery period divided into three 20-second windows
scope_conditions.measurement_type: fNIRS continuous measurement with temporal segmentation

stimulus_description.components: three consecutive recovery phases of 20 seconds each

findings.mechanism: Motor system engagement peaks during mid-recovery (20-40s), reflecting transition phase in recovery dynamics

findings.consequent: Self-reported state anxiety (STAIS-5 scale, 5-20 point range)
findings.statement: Red wall color significantly increased post-recovery anxiety (M=9.05, SD=4.04) compared to baseline (M=6.82, SD=2.43), t(37)=2.92, p<.05

instruments_used.name: Spielberger State-Trait Anxiety Inventory - Short Form
instruments_used.construct_measured: state anxiety (5-item self-report, 4-point Likert scale: 1=not at all to 4=very much so)

findings.quote: red (t (37) = 2.92, p < .05) and purple (t (37) = 2.88, p < .05) significantly increased anxiety relative to baseline

scope_conditions.duration: baseline measured pre-experiment, post-recovery measured after 60-second color exposure
scope_conditions.measurement_type: self-administered scale before and after each color condition

stimulus_description.delivery_method: immersive VR wall color during recovery period

findings.mechanism: Red enhances perceived stress and arousal, impairing subjective recovery despite brief exposure

findings.statement: Purple significantly increased post-recovery anxiety (M=8.66, SD=3.42) relative to baseline (M=6.82, SD=2.43), t(37)=2.88, p<.05
findings.quote: purple (t (37) = 2.88, p < .05) significantly increased anxiety relative to baseline
findings.mechanism: Warm hues (red, purple) maintain arousal and stress-related psychological states

findings.antecedent: Blue, orange, yellow, green, or white wall colors during recovery
findings.statement: Blue (t(37)=-0.31, p=.76), orange (t(37)=1.83, p=.08), yellow (t(37)=0.26, p=.80), green (t(37)=0.58, p=.57), and white (t(37)=0.05, p=.96) wall colors showed no significant change in anxiety relative to baseline
findings.quote: No significant differences were observed for the blue, orange, yellow, green or white conditions (all p > .05)

stimulus_description.components: blue, orange, yellow, green, white monochromatic walls

findings.mechanism: Cool and neutral colors do not sustain stress-related arousal; brief 60-second exposure insufficient for measurable anxiety elevation

findings.antecedent: Red, blue, orange, yellow, green, purple, white wall colors (between-condition comparisons)
findings.statement: Significant main effect of color on overall anxiety: F(6, 222)=6.92, p<.001. Red (M=9.05) and purple (M=8.66) significantly higher than yellow (M=6.97), blue (M=6.66), and white (M=6.84)
findings.quote: A significant main effect of Color was found (F (6, 222) = 6.92, p < .001, η² = 0.16). Post hoc comparisons with FDR correction indicated that the red condition (M = 9.05, SD = 4.04) were significantly higher than in the yellow (M = 6.97, p < .01), blue (M = 6.66, p < .01), and white (M = 6.84, p < .01) conditions
findings.mechanism: Warm hues elicit sustained arousal and anxiety; cool/neutral hues support emotional regulation

theory_links.theory_name: Color psychology - warm hues as activating

findings.antecedent: DLPFC HbO activation levels under yellow wall color condition
findings.statement: Negative correlation between DLPFC activation and anxiety under yellow: r=-.35, p<.05. Increased DLPFC activity associated with lower anxiety
findings.quote: in the yellow condition, DLPFC activation negatively correlated with anxiety (r = −.35)

scope_conditions.measurement_type: correlation between concurrent physiological and psychological measures

findings.mechanism: Cognitive engagement in DLPFC may facilitate emotional regulation under yellow, reducing subjective anxiety

findings.antecedent: PreM&SMC HbO activation levels under white wall color condition
findings.statement: Positive correlation between PreM&SMC activation and anxiety under white: r=.33, p<.05. Increased motor cortex activity associated with higher anxiety
findings.quote: in the white condition, PreM&SMC activation positively correlated with anxiety (r = .33)
findings.mechanism: Elevated motor preparedness under white may reflect compensatory arousal or readiness response accompanying anxiety

findings.antecedent: FEF HbO activation levels under red wall color condition
findings.statement: Positive correlation between FEF activation and anxiety under red: r=.37, p<.05. Enhanced visual attention system activity associated with elevated anxiety
findings.quote: in the red condition, FEF activation positively correlated with STAIS-5 scores (r = .37)

scope_conditions.measurement_type: correlation between FEF activity and anxiety

findings.mechanism: Red-induced enhanced visual salience and threat monitoring through FEF activation drives increased subjective anxiety perception

limitations: Fixed recovery duration (60 seconds) may not capture long-term or cumulative effects of color exposure
Limited sample size (N=38) with university student population may restrict generalizability
Only fNIRS and self-report measures used; physiological signals (heart rate, skin conductance) not incorporated
Within-subject design with randomized color presentation may involve carryover effects despite 60-second inter-block rest periods
VR-based study may not fully translate to real-world built environments due to visual display limitations and immersion differences
Individual differences in color-emotion associations not assessed (color preference, cultural factors)
No assessment of individual response trajectories; only group-level analyses performed

overall_theory_links.description: Environments engaging involuntary attention (low-arousal colors) restore cognitive resources
Warm hues (red) increase arousal and approach motivation; cool hues (blue) reduce arousal
DLPFC engagement supports downregulation of stress-related emotional responses
Red activates threat-detection systems via frontal eye fields and visual attention networks
Built environment features directly modulate neural activity in stress-regulatory circuits

extraction_notes.coverage: All findings from abstract, results, and discussion sections extracted. Findings include both neural (fNIRS) and psychological (STAIS-5) outcomes. Color × Time interaction effects captured separately. Null findings included.
extraction_notes.statistical_precision: All p-values, test statistics, and effect sizes copied directly from tables. FDR correction noted where applied. No values inferred or calculated beyond what reported.
extraction_notes.missing_data: Some correlations in Figure 7 noted as exploratory (not surviving FDR correction); these are captured with caveat in source_quality_indicators. No other significant omissions detected.
